transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?
I came in because I feel wound up almost all the time. It’s like my body is bracing for something bad to happen, even when I’m just sitting at my desk or trying to enjoy dance night.
How long have you been feeling this constant sense of being wound up or on edge—has it been going on for several months, or did it start more recently after something specific happened?
It’s been about nine months now. It started when the condo loan began moving toward foreclosure.
Aside from the foreclosure and finances, do you find yourself worrying excessively about other things too—like your health, relationships, or work performance?

Yes. It doesn’t stay focused on the condo. I’ll start worrying about whether my cousin is upset with me, then whether I’m going to make some mistake on a support call at work, and then about how I’m ever supposed to save money or move forward with my life. It kind of jumps around.
Along with this worry, have you noticed physical symptoms like muscle tension, feeling easily fatigued, trouble concentrating, irritability, or difficulty sleeping?

Yes, concentrating has been hard. At work, I’ll be writing a script or helping someone in English or Spanish, and then I suddenly realize I’m just staring at the screen. My mind has gone to all the things that could go wrong, and I lose my train of thought.
Have you been having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or having restless, unsatisfying sleep?

Most nights, I’m exhausted when I get into bed, but I can’t shut my brain off. I keep replaying the loan notices, work tickets, things I might have missed, and then suddenly it’s two or three in the morning. Even when I do sleep, I wake up feeling like I barely rested.
Have you noticed yourself feeling more irritable or easily annoyed with people over these past several months?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself being especially more irritable with people.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports feeling 'wound up' and on edge nearly continuously for approximately 9 months, with worry that has generalized beyond the initial trigger (foreclosure) to multiple domains including relationships, work performance, and finances. Worry is described as excessive, difficult to control, and free-floating ('jumps around'). Associated symptoms include difficulty concentrating (losing train of thought at work), sleep disturbance (difficulty falling asleep due to racing thoughts, non-restorative sleep), and subjective restlessness/being keyed up. Duration exceeds 6 months, worry spans multiple life areas (not restricted to a single stressor), and symptoms cause functional impact at work. While the anxiety began in the context of a financial stressor (foreclosure), the worry has since generalized well beyond that single issue, which argues against Adjustment Disorder and supports a primary Generalized Anxiety Disorder diagnosis. No discrete panic attacks were described, arguing against Panic Disorder.
